claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy is chemically disordered.
The target alloy is a thin film with a high surface-to-volume ratio.
Controlled post-deposition annealing can enhance short-range chemical ordering in the target alloy.
Enhanced short-range chemical ordering reduces local strain inhomogeneities.
Reduced local strain inhomogeneity moderates nucleation and propagation of the first-order magnetostructural transition.
Local stress concentrations in the as-deposited material cause abrupt, spatially inhomogeneous nucleation events.
Abrupt, inhomogeneous nucleation is responsible for a sharp and hysteretic first-order transition.
Smoothing the magnetostructural transition broadens the magnetocaloric response over temperature.
Smoothing the magnetostructural transition reduces hysteretic energy losses.
Annealed samples will retain a comparably high entropy change while spreading the magnetocaloric effect over a wider temperature range.
Annealed samples will exhibit significantly lower hysteresis losses than as-deposited samples during low-field cycling.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type films exhibit a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type films exhibit substantial hysteresis.
Microstructural heterogeneity limits the heat-exchange efficiency of the as-deposited films.
There is an annealing-temperature and duration window that enhances ordering without causing phase decomposition or excessive grain growth.
Substantial changes in film thickness may cause behavior outside the predicted regime.
A thermal budget near the operating-cycle temperatures can reconfigure local atomic arrangements without causing deleterious phase changes.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes treatments that cause phase decomposition or grain coarsening from the prediction's valid regime, but the falsification rule treats observation of such deleterious phase changes as falsifying the hypothesis. A result outside the stated boundary cannot by itself decisively falsify the bounded hypothesis.
